definition: The flow of electric charge around a circuit. Measured in amperes (A). Symbol: I.
The potential difference between two points in a circuit — the energy transferred per unit charge. Measured in volts (V). Symbol: V.
The opposition to the flow of current in a circuit. Measured in ohms (Ω). Symbol: R.
The relationship between voltage, current and resistance: V = IR. Applies to ohmic conductors at constant temperature.
A component where current is directly proportional to voltage at constant temperature — its resistance stays constant. Example: a resistor.
A property of particles that causes them to experience a force in an electric field. Measured in coulombs (C). Q = It.
A circuit where components are connected in a single loop. Current is the same throughout. Voltage is shared between components.
A circuit where components are connected in separate branches. Voltage is the same across each branch. Current is shared.
A device used to measure current. Connected in series in a circuit.
A device used to measure potential difference (voltage). Connected in parallel across a component.
A component whose resistance decreases as temperature increases. Used in temperature sensors.
Light-dependent resistor — a component whose resistance decreases as light intensity increases. Used in light sensors.
A component that allows current to flow in one direction only. Has very high resistance in reverse.
Light-emitting diode — a diode that emits light when current flows through it. Used as an indicator.
A bulb that produces light by heating a thin wire (filament) until it glows. Its resistance increases with temperature — non-ohmic.
A graph of current against voltage for a component, showing how resistance changes. Shape reveals whether the component is ohmic or non-ohmic.
Electric current that flows in one direction only. Produced by batteries and cells.
Electric current that regularly reverses direction. Mains electricity in the UK is AC at 50 Hz and 230 V.
The brown wire in a plug that carries the alternating current from the supply. Dangerous — at high voltage.
The blue wire in a plug that completes the circuit back to the supply. At approximately 0 V.
The green and yellow striped wire in a plug that provides a safety path for current if a fault occurs. Prevents electric shock.
A safety device containing a thin wire that melts and breaks the circuit if the current exceeds a safe level.
An automatic safety switch that trips and breaks the circuit when the current becomes too large. Can be reset unlike a fuse.
The rate at which energy is transferred. P = IV or P = I²R. Measured in watts (W).
The total energy used by a device. E = Pt or E = QV. Measured in joules (J) or kilowatt-hours (kWh).
A unit of energy used by electricity suppliers. 1 kWh = the energy transferred by a 1 kW device operating for 1 hour.
The system of cables and transformers that distributes electricity from power stations to homes and businesses across the UK.
A transformer that increases voltage and decreases current for efficient transmission of electricity across the National Grid.
A transformer that decreases voltage to a safe level for use in homes and businesses.
A build-up of electric charge on the surface of an insulating material, caused by friction transferring electrons between surfaces.
A region around a charged object where another charged object experiences a force. Field lines point from positive to negative.
